title: How to Figure Out Space Complexity
description: Learn how to analyze and calculate the space complexity of algorithms, including auxiliary space

blocks.text: Most programmers learn time complexity first and treat space complexity as an afterthought. That's a mistake. In real systems and DSA interviews, both matter equally and often you'll be asked to trade one for the other.
This guide takes you from zero to fully confident in analyzing space complexity.
Space complexity measures how much extra memory your algorithm uses as the input size grows.
Just like time complexity, we express it in Big O notation. And just like time, we care about the shape of growth, not the exact bytes.
Two things eat memory in a program:
1. Input space: the memory used to store the input itself. Most of the time we don't count this it's given to us, we didn't create it.
2. Auxiliary space: the extra memory your algorithm creates to do its work. This is what space complexity usually refers to.
When someone says "solve this in O(1) space", they mean: use a constant amount of extra memory, regardless of input size.

items: Rule 1: Only count extra memory you allocate. Input data is already in memory. You didn't allocate it. Don't count it unless the problem says to.
Rule 2: Count the call stack for recursion. Every recursive function call adds a frame to the call stack. That stack is real memory.
Rule 3: Drop constants, keep the dominant term. Same as time complexity. O(2n) → O(n).

content.title: 4. How to Read Code and Find Space Complexity

blocks.text: Follow these patterns every time you see a piece of code.
Pattern 1: A Few Variables
You created one variable. It doesn't matter ifaandbare huge numbers —resultis still just one slot of memory.O(1) space.
The loop runs n times, but you're reusing the same variable total each time. No new memory is being created as n grows. O(1) auxiliary space.
Key insight: a loop alone does not mean O(n) space. It only becomes O(n) space if you're storing something each iteration.
Pattern 2: Creating a New Array or List
How many pairs can you get from n elements? Up to n(n-1)/2 which is O(n²). The pairs list grows quadratically. O(n²)space.
Pattern 3: A Hash Map or Set
In the worst case (all unique elements), the dictionary hasnentries.O(n) space.
Same idea the set can grow up to n items. O(n) space. This is the classic time-vs-space trade-off: you buy O(n) speed by spending O(n) memory.
Pattern 4: A 2D Matrix or Grid
You created n rows, each with n columns. Total cells: n × n. O(n²) space.
This shows up in dynamic programming tables, graph adjacency matrices, and image processing.
Pattern 5: Recursion and the Call Stack
This is the most commonly missed source of space complexity.

Every time a function calls itself, a new stack frame is pushed onto the call stack. That frame stores local variables, the return address, and parameters. When the recursion unwinds, the frames are popped.
The space used = maximum depth of the call stack.

There are n frames on the stack simultaneously at the deepest point. O(n) space even though you're not creating any arrays or variables.
Example 2: Binary recursion (naive Fibonacci):
Even though this creates 2ⁿ total calls (making it O(2ⁿ) time), the stack depth at any moment is at most n because you go all the way down one branch before coming back. O(n) space.
Example 3: Binary search (recursive):
Each call halves the search space. Maximum stack depth = log n. O(log n) space.
Pattern 6: Recursion That Builds a Return Value
Two things are happening here:

items: The call stack goes n levels deep → O(n) stack space
Each call creates a new partial list → O(n) for the slices across all frames

blocks.text: Total: O(n) space (both sources are linear, they don't multiply here).

blocks.text: Trees come up constantly in DSA. Let's be precise.
DFS (Depth-First Search): recursive:
The call stack goes as deep as the tree's height h.

items: Skewed tree (like a linked list): height = n → O(n) space

blocks.text: BFS (Breadth-First Search) — using a queue:
The queue holds at most one entire level of the tree at a time.
Interesting flip: BFS and DFS trade space behaviour depending on tree shape.

content.title: 8. The 5 Questions to Ask for Space Complexity

blocks.text: Just like with time complexity, use a checklist:

items: Are you creating any new variables, arrays, or data structures? If yes → what is their size relative to n?
Does a data structure grow inside a loop? A loop that appends n items = O(n) space.
Is there recursion? If yes → what is the maximum call stack depth?
Are you making copies of the input? arr[:] in Python = a copy = O(n) space.
What is the dominant space consumer? Add them up if independent, then keep the biggest term.
Mistake 1: Forgetting the call stack. "I don't create any arrays in my recursive function, so it's O(1) space." Wrong. Every recursive call takes stack space. The stack is real memory.

Mistake 2: Counting input space. "My function takes an array of n elements, so it's O(n) space." Not necessarily. If you don't create anything new, it's O(1) auxiliary space. The input was already there.
Mistake 3: Assuming in-place means O(1). Sorting in-place is usually O(1) extra space, but recursive in-place algorithms (like recursive quicksort) still use O(log n) call stack space.
Mistake 4: Missing implicit copies. String concatenation in a loop, list slicing, and string slicing all create new objects in memory. s = s + char inside a loop is O(n²) space total, not O(1).

Mistake 5: Confusing space complexity with memory usage. Space complexity is about growth relative to input size, not absolute bytes. A function using 10MB but O(1) growth is fine at scale. A function using 1KB but O(n²) growth is a disaster at scale.

content.title: 11. The One Thing to Remember

blocks.text: Space complexity = the maximum extra memory your algorithm holds at any one moment, as a function of input size.
Count new data structures. Count the call stack. Drop constants. Keep the dominant term.
Master these two time and space and you have the fundamental vocabulary for every DSA conversation, every technical interview, and every system design decision you'll ever face.
